title: Permission sets on EnumSet

blocks.text: An `EnumSet` is a bit vector: one bit per constant, so `contains`, `add` and `retainAll` are single bitwise operations, and it iterates in declaration order. The page builds a permission system on it, and names two pitfalls:

items: An empty `EnumSet` comes from `EnumSet.noneOf(Permission.class)`. `EnumSet.of()` needs at least one element, and `EnumSet.copyOf` of an empty plain collection throws, because it cannot tell the enum type.
`public static final Set<Permission> ALL = EnumSet.allOf(...)` hands every caller a mutable set. Wrap shared sets so nobody can change them.

blocks.text: Complete `Permission { READ, WRITE, EXECUTE, DELETE, ADMIN }`:

items: The four shared sets: `READ_ONLY` = {READ}, `READ_WRITE` = {READ, WRITE}, `FULL_ACCESS` = every permission, `NO_ACCESS` = none. Callers cannot change them.
`static Set<Permission> combine(Set<Permission>... sets)`: the union of the sets; no sets, or only empty ones, give an empty set.
`static Set<Permission> intersect(Set<Permission>... sets)`: the permissions every set holds; no sets at all give an empty set.

cases.says: The named sets hold the right permissions, combine() is their union and intersect() their intersection, each in declaration order.
combine() of no sets, or of empty sets only, is an empty set rather than an exception.
intersect() of no sets at all, or starting with an empty plain set, is an empty set rather than an exception.
None of the four public named sets (READ_ONLY, READ_WRITE, FULL_ACCESS, NO_ACCESS) can be changed by callers.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: EnumSet represents permission flags, an empty one comes from noneOf, and shared sets are wrapped as unmodifiable.
